text: Document loading and preprocessing is the first step of a retrieval pipeline. Raw text is read from files or databases, cleaned of noise such as extra whitespace, and normalized before it can be chunked.
Fixed-size chunking splits a document into pieces of a set number of words or tokens. It is simple to implement and works well as a baseline strategy for many retrieval tasks.
Chunk overlap means that consecutive chunks share a few words at their boundary. This helps preserve context that would otherwise be lost when a sentence is cut in half between two chunks.

Semantic boundary chunking splits text at natural breakpoints such as paragraphs or sentences instead of a fixed word count, which can produce chunks that are easier for a language model to reason about.
Vector embeddings represent a piece of text as a list of numbers in a high dimensional space, where pieces of text with similar meaning end up close together in that space.

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and is the most common way to compare embeddings for similarity search. A score close to 1 means the vectors point in nearly the same direction, while a score close to 0 means they are unrelated.
A vector store is a database that holds chunk embeddings alongside their original text, allowing a query embedding to be compared quickly against every stored chunk.

Top-k retrieval returns the k chunks whose embeddings are most similar to the query embedding. Choosing a larger k gives the language model more context but also increases the risk of including irrelevant information.
Chunk size has a direct tradeoff with retrieval quality. Very small chunks may lack enough context on their own, while very large chunks can dilute the relevant information with unrelated text.
Irrelevant retrieved chunks happen when the similarity search returns text that does not actually answer the query, often because the chunk boundaries split up related ideas.
Missing context in a RAG system occurs when none of the retrieved chunks contain the specific fact needed to answer the question, even though the answer exists somewhere in the corpus.
Redundant chunks appear when overlapping or duplicate passages from the corpus are retrieved together, wasting space in the context window without adding new information.
